content.value: A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. Containers isolate applications from each other and from the host system.
Think of it like shipping containers in real life — a standardized box that can hold anything and be transported anywhere. Software containers work the same way: "Build once, run anywhere."

content.title: Containers vs Virtual Machines
content.value:
graph TB
    subgraph VM ["Virtual Machine"]
        VA["App A"] & VB["App B"]
        VLA["Libs A"] & VLB["Libs B"]
        VGA["Guest OS"] & VGB["Guest OS"]
        VH["Hypervisor"]
        VHW["Hardware"]
    end
    subgraph CT ["Container"]
        CA["App A"] & CB["App B"]
        CLA["Libs A"] & CLB["Libs B"]
        CE["Container Engine (Docker)"]
        CHO["Host OS Kernel"]
        CHW["Hardware"]
    end
    style VM fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style CT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
Key interview fact: Containers share the host OS kernel while VMs each run their own kernel. This makes containers 10-100x lighter (MBs vs GBs) and faster to start (seconds vs minutes) than VMs.

quiz.question: What is the main architectural difference between containers and VMs?
options: Containers are more secure than VMs
Containers share the host kernel; VMs run their own kernel
VMs are faster than containers
Containers need a hypervisor
quiz.explanation: Containers share the host OS kernel and only package the application layer. VMs virtualize the hardware and run a complete guest OS, making them heavier.

content.value: Docker uses a client-server architecture. You type commands into the **Docker Client** (CLI), which sends HTTP API requests to the **Docker Daemon** (dockerd), which does the actual work of building, running, and managing containers.

content.title: Docker Architecture
content.value:
graph LR
    CLI["🖥️ Docker CLI\n(docker run, build)"] -->|REST API| DAEMON["⚙️ Docker Daemon\n(dockerd)"]
    DAEMON --> IMAGES["📦 Images\n(Blueprints)"]
    DAEMON --> CONTAINERS["🏃 Containers\n(Running instances)"]
    DAEMON --> NETWORKS["🌐 Networks\n(Communication)"]
    DAEMON --> VOLUMES["💾 Volumes\n(Persistent storage)"]
    DAEMON <-->|pull/push| REGISTRY["☁️ Docker Hub\n(Registry)"]
    style CLI fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style DAEMON fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style REGISTRY fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0

**Image** — A read-only template containing your application code, runtime, libraries, and configuration. Think of it as a class in OOP.

**Container** — A running instance of an image. Think of it as an object created from the class. You can have many containers from one image.

**Registry** — A storage service for Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry.

content.title: Essential Docker Commands
content.value:
docker pull nginx              # Download an image from Docker Hub
docker images                  # List all local images
docker run nginx               # Create and start a container
docker run -d -p 80:80 nginx   # Run detached, map port 80
docker ps                      # List running containers
docker ps -a                   # List ALL containers (including stopped)
docker stop <container_id>     # Stop a running container
docker rm <container_id>       # Remove a stopped container
docker logs <container_id>     # View container logs
docker exec -it <id> /bin/sh   # Open a shell inside a container

quiz.question: What is the relationship between a Docker image and a container?
options: They are the same thing
An image is a running instance of a container
A container is a running instance of an image
Images run on containers
quiz.explanation: An image is a static blueprint (like a class). A container is a running instance created from that image (like an object). You can create many containers from one image.

content.value: A Dockerfile is a text file with instructions to build a Docker image. Each instruction creates a layer in the image, and Docker caches these layers for faster rebuilds. Think of it as a recipe — each step builds on the previous one.

content.title: Dockerfile Build Process
content.value:
graph TD
    A["FROM node:18-alpine"] -->|Layer 1: Base image| B["WORKDIR /app"]
    B -->|Layer 2: Set directory| C["COPY package*.json ./"]
    C -->|Layer 3: Copy deps file| D["RUN npm install"]
    D -->|Layer 4: Install deps ⚡ CACHED| E["COPY . ."]
    E -->|Layer 5: Copy source code| F["CMD node server.js"]
    F --> G["🐳 Final Image"]
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style D fill:#162231,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style G fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Example Dockerfile
content.value:
# Start from a base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency files first (for caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm install --production

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

Interview tip: Copying package.json before the rest of the code is a Dockerfile best practice. If your code changes but dependencies don't, Docker reuses the cached npm install layer — saving minutes on each build.

content.title: Build and Run
content.value:
docker build -t myapp:v1 .              # Build image, tag as myapp:v1
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp:v1     # Run the container
docker image ls                         # List all images with sizes

quiz.question: Why should you COPY package.json before COPY . . in a Dockerfile?
options: It doesn't matter — the order is irrelevant
To leverage Docker's layer caching — dependencies are reinstalled only when package.json changes
Because package.json must be read first
To prevent security vulnerabilities
quiz.explanation: Docker caches each layer. If package.json hasn't changed, the npm install layer is reused from cache. If you copy everything first, any code change invalidates the cache and forces a full reinstall.

content.value: By default, containers are isolated from each other. Docker provides **networking** to let containers communicate (like connecting offices with phone lines), and **volumes** to persist data beyond the container lifecycle (like saving files to a USB drive that survives a computer restart).

content.title: Docker Networking Model
content.value:
graph TB
    subgraph NET ["Custom Network: mynet"]
        APP["🌐 App Container\nName: app\nPort: 3000"] <-->|"app:3000"| DB["🗄️ Database Container\nName: db\nPort: 5432"]
        APP <-->|"cache:6379"| CACHE["⚡ Redis Container\nName: cache\nPort: 6379"]
    end
    HOST["💻 Host Machine"] -->|"localhost:3000 → app:3000"| APP
    style NET fill:#0f1923,stroke:#00d4ff33,color:#e2e8f0
    style APP fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style DB fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style CACHE fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Docker Networking
content.value:
docker network ls                          # List networks
docker network create mynet                # Create a custom network
docker run -d --name db --network mynet postgres    # Run on custom network
docker run -d --name app --network mynet myapp      # Same network = can communicate

# 'app' can now reach 'db' by container name:
# postgres://db:5432/mydb
On a custom Docker network, containers can reach each other using container names as hostnames. This is how microservices communicate in Docker Compose.

content.title: Docker Volumes
content.value:
docker volume create mydata                          # Create a named volume
docker run -v mydata:/data postgres                  # Mount volume at /data
docker run -v $(pwd)/config:/app/config myapp        # Bind mount: host dir → container

# Volumes persist data even after the container is deleted
docker volume ls                                     # List all volumes
docker volume inspect mydata                         # See volume details

quiz.question: How can two Docker containers on the same custom network communicate?
options: They cannot — containers are always isolated
By using the host's IP address
By using container names as hostnames
Only through shared volumes
quiz.explanation: On a user-defined Docker network, containers can resolve each other by name. 'docker run --name db --network mynet postgres' can be reached at hostname 'db' by other containers on 'mynet'.

content.value: Real applications are never a single container. A typical web app might have: a frontend, a backend API, a database, and a cache. **Docker Compose** lets you define and run all these containers together with a single YAML file and a single command.

content.title: docker-compose.yml Example
content.value:
version: '3.8'

services:
  api:
    build: ./server
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
      - REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379
    depends_on:
      - db
      - cache
    networks:
      - app-network

  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - app-network

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    networks:
      - app-network

volumes:
  db-data:

networks:
  app-network:

content.title: Docker Compose Commands
content.value:
docker compose up              # Start all services
docker compose up -d           # Start in detached (background) mode
docker compose down            # Stop and remove all containers
docker compose logs -f api     # Follow logs for the 'api' service
docker compose ps              # List running services
docker compose build           # Rebuild images
docker compose exec api sh     # Open shell in running 'api' container

Interview tip: depends_on only waits for the container to START, not for the application inside to be READY. For production, use healthchecks to ensure the database is actually accepting connections before the API tries to connect.

quiz.question: What does 'docker compose up -d' do?
options: Deletes all containers
Starts all services defined in docker-compose.yml in detached (background) mode
Downloads Docker Compose
Shows container logs
quiz.explanation: 'docker compose up' creates and starts all containers defined in the Compose file. The '-d' flag runs them in the background so you get your terminal back.

content.value: Multi-stage builds are a Dockerfile technique where you use multiple FROM statements to separate the **build environment** from the **runtime environment**. This dramatically reduces your final image size because build tools, compilers, and dev dependencies are left behind.

content.title: Multi-Stage Build Flow
content.value:
graph LR
    subgraph STAGE1 ["Stage 1: Builder (1.2 GB)"]
        S1A["Node.js + npm"] --> S1B["Install ALL deps"]
        S1B --> S1C["Compile & Build"]
    end
    subgraph STAGE2 ["Stage 2: Production (85 MB)"]
        S2A["Alpine base only"] --> S2B["Copy built output"]
        S2B --> S2C["Production deps only"]
    end
    S1C -->|COPY --from=builder| S2B
    style STAGE1 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style STAGE2 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Multi-Stage Dockerfile (React + Node.js)
content.value:
# ---- Stage 1: Build ----
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                      # Install ALL dependencies (including devDependencies)
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                # Compile React/TypeScript → static files

# ---- Stage 2: Production ----
FROM node:18-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # Only production dependencies
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

The result: Your build stage might be 1.2 GB with all the compilers and dev tools. But the final production image is only 85 MB — containing just the compiled output and production runtime. This means faster deployments, smaller attack surface, and lower cloud costs.
Use 'npm ci' instead of 'npm install' in Dockerfiles. 'npm ci' installs exact versions from package-lock.json and is faster and more reliable for CI/CD environments.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of multi-stage Docker builds?
options: They make containers run faster
They allow using multiple programming languages
They dramatically reduce final image size by separating build tools from runtime
They are required by Docker Hub
quiz.explanation: Multi-stage builds separate the heavy build environment (compilers, dev deps) from the lightweight production image. Only the compiled output is copied to the final stage, resulting in much smaller images.

content.value: Security is critical when running containers in production. A misconfigured container can expose your entire host system. Here are the essential security practices every DevOps engineer must follow.

content.title: Container Security Layers
content.value:
graph TD
    A["🔒 Image Security"] --> A1["Use official base images"]
    A --> A2["Scan for vulnerabilities"]
    A --> A3["Use minimal base (Alpine)"]
    B["👤 Runtime Security"] --> B1["Run as non-root user"]
    B --> B2["Read-only filesystem"]
    B --> B3["Drop capabilities"]
    C["🌐 Network Security"] --> C1["Limit exposed ports"]
    C --> C2["Use internal networks"]
    C --> C3["Never expose Docker socket"]
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Secure Dockerfile Example
content.value:
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create a non-root user
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup . .

# Switch to non-root user
USER appuser

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

content.title: Security Commands
content.value:
# Scan images for vulnerabilities
docker scout cves myapp:latest

# Run with read-only filesystem
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp

# Run with limited capabilities
docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE myapp

# Never do this in production!
docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock  # DANGEROUS!

Never run containers as root in production! If an attacker escapes the container, they'll have root access to your host machine. Always create and switch to a non-root user with the USER directive in your Dockerfile.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid running containers as root?
options: Root containers are slower
Root containers use more memory
If an attacker escapes the container, they'd have root access to the host system
Docker doesn't support root containers
quiz.explanation: Running as root is a security risk. If a container is compromised, the attacker could potentially break out and gain root access to the host machine. Always use a non-root USER in your Dockerfile.

content.value: When containers misbehave in production, you need a systematic approach to diagnose and fix issues. Here's the debugging toolkit every DevOps engineer needs.

content.title: Container Debugging Flowchart
content.value:
graph TD
    START["🚨 Container Problem"] --> Q1{"Is it running?"}
    Q1 -->|No| A1["docker ps -a\nCheck exit code"]
    A1 --> A2["docker logs container_id\nRead error messages"]
    Q1 -->|Yes but unhealthy| B1["docker logs -f container_id\nWatch live logs"]
    B1 --> B2["docker exec -it id sh\nShell into container"]
    B2 --> B3["docker stats\nCheck CPU/Memory"]
    A2 --> FIX["🔧 Fix and Redeploy"]
    B3 --> FIX
    style START fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style FIX fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Debugging Commands
content.value:
# Step 1: Check container status and exit codes
docker ps -a                              # See all containers + exit status
# Exit code 0 = normal exit
# Exit code 1 = application error
# Exit code 137 = killed (OOM or SIGKILL)
# Exit code 143 = graceful termination (SIGTERM)

# Step 2: Read logs
docker logs <container_id>                # Full log output
docker logs --tail 50 <container_id>      # Last 50 lines
docker logs -f <container_id>             # Follow logs in real-time

# Step 3: Shell into a running container
docker exec -it <container_id> /bin/sh    # Open interactive shell

# Step 4: Inspect container details
docker inspect <container_id>             # Full JSON config + network info
docker stats                              # Live CPU/Memory/Network usage

# Step 5: Debug a crashing container
docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh myapp  # Override CMD to get a shell

Pro debugging trick: If a container keeps crashing on startup, override the entrypoint to get a shell: 'docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh myapp'. This lets you poke around inside the container's filesystem and run the app manually to see the real error.

quiz.question: A container exits with code 137. What happened?
options: The application had a bug
The container was killed (likely Out of Memory or SIGKILL)
The Dockerfile was invalid
The port was already in use
quiz.explanation: Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). This usually means the container ran out of memory and was killed by the kernel's OOM killer, or someone manually ran 'docker kill'.
